title: what your grandmother was actually doing
hookLine: Krishna's poor friend Sudama brings a bundle of rice; why a flower and a cup of water make a whole puja
tomorrow: the thing that's yours to do

cards: Two boys once studied under the same teacher: Krishna, a prince, and a poor brahmin boy remembered as Sudama. Years later Krishna is a king in Dwaraka, and Sudama's family is going hungry.
His wife begs him: go and see your old friend. He has nothing to bring, so she begs four handfuls of flattened rice from the neighbors, and he ties them into his worn cloth.
At the palace, Krishna runs to hug him, washes his feet, and seats him on his own bed. Then he asks: what did you bring me? Sudama is too ashamed to hand over cheap rice.
So Krishna finds it himself, pulls it loose, and eats a handful with joy.

teach.h: A LEAF, A FLOWER, A FRUIT, WATER
teach.b: This old story holds today's word: puja, the way Hindus worship God with their hands.
Before Krishna takes the rice, he says a line many Hindus know by heart, from the Bhagavad Gita: whoever offers me a leaf, a flower, a fruit, or water, with devotion, I accept it.
In Sanskrit it begins: patram pushpam phalam toyam. Nothing on that list costs much.
What God receives is the devotion, bhakti, the heart tied up in the gift. Now look at a home puja.
Many follow the steps of welcoming an honored guest, the way Krishna welcomed Sudama: a seat, water for the feet, water to sip. Then a flower, incense, a waved lamp, a bell, and food.
Afterward the food comes back as prasad, a gift from God, shared and eaten. A shrine can be a whole room or one shelf with a picture and a lamp.

teach.h: THE SIZE WAS NEVER THE POINT
teach.b: That's the teaching: in Hinduism, the size of the offering was never the point. A marigold and a cup of water, offered with love, is a whole puja.
What you're really bringing is yourself: your care, your attention, for a few minutes given to God. So a grandmother at that shelf before the kettle goes on isn't only keeping a custom.
Like Sudama, she's bringing what she has, and it's enough.

how: At a home shrine, a devotee may offer water, flowers, incense, a waved lamp and food, ring a bell, and then share the food as prasad; temple priests perform puja in the same spirit on a larger scale.

games.q: Nani's staying with us 2 wks!! Sam slept over and saw her puja at 6am, water, a flower, a sweet. Sam goes 'is she feeding a statue?' 😭 help
o: she's offering love, not lunch. like Sudama's rice: Krishna took it for the heart in it. and the sweet comes back to us as prasad.
honestly it's an old superstition. don't overthink it.
it only counts if it's expensive, so Nani's doing it wrong.
games.why: Krishna ate Sudama's cheap rice with joy for the love tied up in it. In puja the devotion is the offering, and the food comes back as prasad.

games.q: match the story to the puja.
p: the gift he was ashamed of
a leaf, a flower: offered with love

s: a puja needs an expensive offering
a leaf, a flower, a fruit, water, offered with devotion, is enough. Krishna ate Sudama's cheap rice with joy.
Krishna ate the rice his friend was ashamed to give
he pulled the bundle from Sudama's cloth and ate a handful.
the food offered in puja is thrown away
it comes back as prasad, a gift to be shared and eaten.

games.q: you want to make an offering, and all you have in the house is a glass of water. what does the Gita say about it?
o: wait until you can afford something better.
games.why: a leaf, a flower, a fruit, water, offered with devotion, is accepted. Krishna took Sudama's handful of rice the same way. the cost was never the point.

practice: Here's the practice, the smallest puja there is. If you have a shrine or a picture of God, set one thing before it: a flower, a cup of water, a piece of fruit. If you don't, set something you love in front of you.
Look at it first. Then offer it with both hands, and give it your full attention. If you pray, say silently: this is for you.
If you don't, just let one thing have all of you for a while. The bell holds the time.

wordCard.voice: Puja. Worship with the hands: water, a flower, a flame, food, offered with devotion. Eighth word.

orig.note: Sanskrit: honor, worship; care offered to God, often through the senses.

carryVoice: Your line: attention is an offering. Krishna wanted the rice for the love tied up in it. Give one thing today your whole attention, and you've given what matters. Day eight.

sources.ref: Bhagavata Purana 10.80–10.81 (Sudama brings Krishna flattened rice; 10.81.4 repeats Gita 9.26)
